nodes.label: Infrastructure investment in digital platforms
nodes.slide_anchor_title: Infrastructure and Scale in Digital Platforms
nodes.source_sentence: One of the slides I think I shared with you was hyperscaler spent on CapEx. So this is one of the interesting stories at the moment.
nodes.description: Spending money to build and improve the technology and hardware that support digital services, like servers and networks.
nodes.why_it_matters: Understanding infrastructure investment helps explain why digital platforms can scale and offer reliable services, and why these investments are crucial for growth.

nodes.label: Cloud and data center capacity
nodes.slide_anchor_title: Infrastructure and Scale in Digital Platforms
nodes.source_sentence: OpenAI is committed to spending. I think it's 100 billion over the next five years on AI infrastructure, and they capitalise there.
nodes.description: The total amount of computing power and storage available in cloud services and data centers.
nodes.why_it_matters: Cloud and data center capacity determines how much digital work can be handled, affecting performance, scalability, and the ability to support new technologies like AI.

nodes.label: Data center efficiency
nodes.slide_anchor_title: Infrastructure and Scale in Digital Platforms
nodes.source_sentence: which is why data centre efficiency is such a big thing at the moment.
nodes.description: How effectively a data center uses its resources, such as energy and hardware, to deliver services.
nodes.why_it_matters: Improving data center efficiency reduces costs and environmental impact, making digital services more sustainable and affordable.

nodes.label: Pricing strategy
nodes.source_sentence: Now what does that mean? Which brings us into one of the big topics is if you're marginal cost to zero, and you've got all these different ways that we can deliver value over time, what does that mean for pricing and what is a fair price?
nodes.description: The approach a company uses to set prices for its products or services.
nodes.why_it_matters: Pricing strategy directly affects revenue, competitiveness, and how customers perceive value, making it a key business decision.

nodes.label: Price discovery mechanisms
nodes.source_sentence: So the question is, what are the mechanisms we can put in place to discover what our pricing should be, what has value to the customer, and then how can we discover which customers value things at different levels?
nodes.description: Methods used to figure out the best price for a product or service based on customer demand and value.
nodes.why_it_matters: Effective price discovery helps businesses maximize profits and ensure customers feel they're getting fair value.

nodes.label: Tiered pricing
nodes.source_sentence: If we're in the enterprise space, that's where you start to get price tiering, which becomes really important.
nodes.description: A pricing approach where different versions or levels of a product are offered at different prices.
nodes.why_it_matters: Tiered pricing allows companies to serve different customer needs and budgets, increasing market reach and revenue.

nodes.label: Freemium model
nodes.source_sentence: If you're in the freemium market, if you don't pay us anything, you can download the software anyway if you want service or hosting that goes along with that will charge you a bit more if you want.
nodes.description: A business model where basic services are free, but users pay for advanced features or services.
nodes.why_it_matters: The freemium model helps attract a large user base and can convert free users into paying customers over time.

nodes.label: Price before product
nodes.source_sentence: Maddy has a wonderful talk which is on the first round, Capital Review, which is essentially its price before product period.
nodes.description: The idea of deciding on a product's price before finalizing its features or design.
nodes.why_it_matters: Setting price before product helps ensure that what you build matches what customers are willing to pay, reducing risk.

nodes.label: Lifetime value of a customer
nodes.source_sentence: if you're looking at lifetime value, lifetime value is revenue minus retention.
nodes.description: The total profit a company expects to earn from a customer over the entire relationship.
nodes.why_it_matters: Knowing customer lifetime value helps businesses decide how much to invest in acquiring and keeping customers.

nodes.label: Special pricing for customer segments
nodes.source_sentence: I'm still trying to sign up to the Apple Creator student educational discount because they're very aware that if you if they get you as a student and you build your work habits and your practices around something, they tend to retain you over time.
nodes.description: Offering unique pricing deals to specific groups, like students or educators.
nodes.why_it_matters: Special pricing can attract and retain valuable customer segments, building long-term loyalty.

nodes.label: Pricing complexity
nodes.source_sentence: every system accumulates cruft over time as you do a special price here, or you do a special version of your software, you do a free discount. Try and keep that as minimal as possible because complexity creates problems.
nodes.description: The complications that arise when a business offers many different prices, discounts, or versions of a product.
nodes.why_it_matters: Managing pricing complexity is important because too much complexity can confuse customers and make systems harder to maintain.

nodes.label: Merchant systems
nodes.source_sentence: So there are some very basic practicalities and we've touched on most of these before. When are you going to require people to log on. Are you going to store things. Same process, all of these things. You've got to not only build a system that can manage it, but you've got to build a system that you can have human beings navigate and then explain to customers and then explain and training situation.
nodes.description: The systems and processes businesses use to handle sales, payments, and customer transactions.
nodes.why_it_matters: Efficient merchant systems are essential for smooth sales operations and good customer experiences.

nodes.label: Legacy system integration
nodes.source_sentence: And as time goes on, managing your legacy becomes even more complicated.
nodes.description: The process of connecting and managing older technology systems with newer ones.
nodes.why_it_matters: Legacy system integration is important because many businesses rely on old systems that must work with modern technology.

nodes.label: Batch processing in legacy systems
nodes.source_sentence: A lot of legacy systems are essentially batch processing systems, but they run it when they've got excess capacity.
nodes.description: A method where legacy systems process data in large groups at scheduled times, rather than instantly.
nodes.why_it_matters: Understanding batch processing helps explain the limitations and challenges of older systems in today's fast-paced digital world.

nodes.label: Documentation and maintainability of systems
nodes.source_sentence: How well documented as your system is, is will your documentation manage 30 years worth of programmers messing with it, shall we say?
nodes.description: How well a system is documented and how easy it is to update or fix over time.
nodes.why_it_matters: Good documentation and maintainability ensure that systems can be improved and repaired, even as staff changes.

nodes.label: Payment infrastructure
nodes.source_sentence: Credit cards, customer care and XML. It's really kind of EDI. How do we get systems to talk to each other?
nodes.description: The technology and processes that allow businesses to accept and manage electronic payments.
nodes.why_it_matters: Reliable payment infrastructure is crucial for online businesses to operate smoothly and securely.

nodes.label: Fraud and transaction risk
nodes.source_sentence: Everyone has a credit card. Horror story.
nodes.description: The risk of fraudulent activity or errors in financial transactions.
nodes.why_it_matters: Managing fraud and transaction risk protects both businesses and customers from financial loss.

nodes.label: Tax compliance in online payments
nodes.source_sentence: And tax is a nightmare. Tax is always a nightmare. What happens if your electronic system that you take on stripe did this in the early days doesn't collect VAT? Then the vat man turns around, says, actually, you owe us 20% of all your sales for the last three years, which they can do.
nodes.description: Making sure online payment systems follow tax laws, like collecting the correct sales tax or VAT.
nodes.why_it_matters: Tax compliance is essential to avoid legal trouble and unexpected costs for online businesses.

nodes.label: Customer Relationship Management
nodes.source_sentence: Which brings us to CRM. There are horror stories around customer health centres for a reason. They can be a nightmare, but if you get them right, it can be amazing.
nodes.description: Systems and strategies for managing a company's interactions with current and potential customers.
nodes.why_it_matters: Effective CRM helps businesses build strong relationships, improve customer satisfaction, and increase sales.

nodes.label: Continuity of customer experience
nodes.source_sentence: And how do we think of continuity in customer experience, especially if your first line support is a call centre in Ireland? Your second line support as a technical user in New York.
nodes.description: Ensuring customers have a consistent and smooth experience across all interactions with a company.
nodes.why_it_matters: Continuity of customer experience builds trust and loyalty, making customers more likely to return.

nodes.label: Customer verification and security questions
nodes.source_sentence: How do we verify who is on the other end of the phone? Often. That's what's your security question? There tends to be 4 or 5 standard security questions.
nodes.description: Customer verification and security questions are methods used to confirm a customer's identity, often by asking standard questions only the real customer should know.
nodes.why_it_matters: Verifying customer identity is crucial for protecting accounts and preventing fraud, especially in online and phone-based services.

nodes.label: Personalisation
nodes.source_sentence: The answer to a lot of this is how do we increase retention is personalisation. You know, how do we make each visit relevant to you?
nodes.description: Personalisation is the process of tailoring products, services, or experiences to individual users based on their preferences or behaviors.
nodes.why_it_matters: Personalisation helps increase customer retention and satisfaction by making each interaction more relevant and engaging.

nodes.label: Demographic segmentation
nodes.source_sentence: So if I know who you are and I know your address and post codes, probably 20 years ago, I could have told you to within £5,000 what your income was for your household.
nodes.description: Demographic segmentation divides customers into groups based on characteristics like age, income, or location.
nodes.why_it_matters: Understanding demographics allows businesses to target their marketing and services more effectively to different customer groups.

nodes.label: Behavioral segmentation
nodes.source_sentence: So we can start to classify people by behavioural patterns instead, which I encourage you to think about, because it really doesn't matter if you're 18 or 35, if you behave the same way on the internet, you can sell or you can buy in the same on the internet.
nodes.description: Behavioral segmentation groups customers based on their actions, such as browsing habits or purchase history.
nodes.why_it_matters: This approach helps businesses predict future behavior and personalize offers, regardless of demographic differences.

nodes.label: Socio-economic classification
nodes.source_sentence: There are then three national socio economic classes which you can look up.
nodes.description: Socio-economic classification sorts people into categories based on their social and economic status.
nodes.why_it_matters: Knowing a customer's socio-economic class can help businesses tailor products and marketing strategies to fit their needs and spending power.

nodes.label: Customer personas
nodes.source_sentence: So if we go traditionally in terms of how do we understand pen portraits, if you're a marketing agent, kind of are the big things. So typically you'll say, here are the five types of people that we want to work with. And you'll pay kind of marketing people to say, these are the big people. And then they'll tend to give them silly names like Super Susan or Sleepy Steve, or these sorts of things to say.
nodes.description: Customer personas are fictional profiles that represent typical users or customers, often given names and characteristics.
nodes.why_it_matters: Personas help teams understand and design for the needs, behaviors, and goals of different customer types.

nodes.label: High-expectation users
nodes.source_sentence: This was kind of put together by Julie, and she points out very properly that in the early times you want to figure out who your super users are, who are your high expectation users, who are the people that will come to your website, use your website and they will influence other people.
nodes.description: High-expectation users are customers who use a product intensively and have high standards, often influencing others.
nodes.why_it_matters: Identifying and satisfying these users can drive product improvement and word-of-mouth growth.

nodes.label: Internationalisation challenges
nodes.source_sentence: Um, internationalisation, just because we're talking about e-commerce, um, is surprisingly difficult and nuanced and culturally dependent.
nodes.description: Internationalisation challenges refer to the difficulties businesses face when expanding to global markets, including cultural and legal differences.
nodes.why_it_matters: Understanding these challenges is essential for successfully adapting products and services for different countries.

nodes.label: Cultural and language differences in internationalisation
nodes.source_sentence: And there are very simple and obvious things down to design what colours are culturally appropriate in different countries. When can you use certain colours? Um, red is particularly valuable in some countries, blue and others, um, just swapping out words for other words are not as simple. Anyone who speaks more than one language will tell you you don't just translate sentences.
nodes.description: Cultural and language differences in internationalisation involve adapting content, design, and communication to fit local customs and languages.
nodes.why_it_matters: Ignoring these differences can lead to misunderstandings or offend customers, hurting a brand's reputation abroad.

nodes.label: Legal and regulatory differences
nodes.source_sentence: What rules? Of which countries do you have to abide by and how are you going to pay for things?
nodes.description: Legal and regulatory differences are the varying laws and rules businesses must follow in different countries.
nodes.why_it_matters: Complying with local laws is necessary to operate legally and avoid penalties when doing business internationally.

nodes.label: Monetisation models
nodes.source_sentence: There are so many different ways that we can essentially do the same thing, but for different ways.
nodes.description: Monetisation models are the different ways a business can earn revenue, such as ads, subscriptions, or pay-per-use.
nodes.why_it_matters: Choosing the right monetisation model is key to a business's financial success and sustainability.

nodes.label: Advertising-funded services
nodes.source_sentence: Funded by adverts is the way that a lot of the internet is funded at the moment. Even if we all hate adverts.
nodes.description: Advertising-funded services are platforms or products that make money by showing ads to users.
nodes.why_it_matters: This model is common online and allows users to access services for free, supported by advertisers.

nodes.label: Subscription and pay-per-use models
nodes.source_sentence: Betting is an obvious one's licensing slash subscriptions.
nodes.description: Subscription and pay-per-use models charge users a recurring fee or a fee each time they use a service.
nodes.why_it_matters: These models provide predictable revenue and can be more appealing to certain customer segments.

nodes.label: Cost per acquisition and lifetime value metrics
nodes.source_sentence: Track CPA what's your cost per acquisition? What's it cost to bring in a new user lifetime value? What do you get out of your customer over the lifetime of their use? And then what's your average revenue per customer?
nodes.description: Cost per acquisition (CPA) and lifetime value (LTV) are metrics that measure how much it costs to gain a customer and how much revenue that customer brings over time.
nodes.why_it_matters: Tracking these metrics helps businesses evaluate the effectiveness and profitability of their marketing and monetisation strategies.

nodes.label: Brand awareness
nodes.source_sentence: Brand awareness becomes super important. This is where a lot of trust comes in.
nodes.description: Brand awareness is how familiar people are with a brand and its products.
nodes.why_it_matters: High brand awareness builds trust and can influence customer choices, making it easier to attract and retain users.

nodes.label: Keyword advertising
nodes.source_sentence: If I'm selling a pair of sneakers, is it okay for me to buy the web search Nike because people looking for sneakers will type in Nike?
nodes.description: Keyword advertising is a marketing strategy where businesses pay to have their ads appear when users search for specific words online.
nodes.why_it_matters: This method targets potential customers who are already interested in related products or services, increasing the chances of sales.

nodes.label: Campaign performance metrics
nodes.source_sentence: So think about click through rates. Think about cost per click. Think about cost per action.
nodes.description: Campaign performance metrics are measurements like click-through rates and cost per click that show how well an advertising campaign is doing.
nodes.why_it_matters: These metrics help businesses understand which campaigns are effective and where to invest their marketing budget.

nodes.label: Network effects
nodes.source_sentence: So if we believe in a world and the online world is like this, where users add value, what is the reputation we want a Facebook user to have? Does the Facebook user have a reputation or is it just everyone in the world? For us, Facebook become the land of boomers and Instagram is where the kids are. So how do we think about that? How do our users represent us and how do we want to benefit from it? But also how do we want to protect ourselves against that?
nodes.description: Network effects occur when a product or service becomes more valuable as more people use it.
nodes.why_it_matters: Network effects can drive rapid growth and make it hard for competitors to catch up, especially in online platforms.

nodes.label: User-generated content
nodes.source_sentence: So consumer generated content.
nodes.description: User-generated content is material like reviews, posts, or videos created by users rather than the company.
nodes.why_it_matters: This content can attract more users, build community, and enhance the value of a platform.

nodes.label: Chicken-and-egg problem in platform adoption
nodes.source_sentence: Chicken and egg Networks. We spoke about this with Bandwagons.
nodes.description: The chicken-and-egg problem in platform adoption is the challenge of attracting users to a new platform when its value depends on having many users already.
nodes.why_it_matters: Solving this problem is crucial for launching successful platforms that rely on user participation.

nodes.label: Disintermediation
nodes.source_sentence: Very quick word about disintermediation. I've mentioned this before. Traditional supply chains had margins and standard margins built into each step. And therefore if you can take certain people out in theory, you can then save that margin.
nodes.description: Disintermediation is the process of removing intermediaries or middlemen from a supply chain, allowing producers to connect directly with consumers.
nodes.why_it_matters: Understanding disintermediation helps explain how businesses can reduce costs and potentially increase profits by cutting out unnecessary steps in the value chain.

nodes.label: Direct producer-to-consumer relationships
nodes.source_sentence: But you've got to be conscious of what was the value each step in that value chain was putting in. Where are they looking after distribution for you? Were they managing consumer relationships?
nodes.description: Direct producer-to-consumer relationships occur when producers sell their products or services straight to consumers, bypassing traditional distribution channels.
nodes.why_it_matters: This concept is important because it highlights both the opportunities and challenges that come with removing intermediaries, such as taking on new responsibilities like distribution and customer management.

nodes.label: Analytics and data-driven strategy
nodes.source_sentence: As we instrument everything, we will get every data under the sun to tell us whatever story we want it to tell us.
nodes.description: Analytics and data-driven strategy involve using data to guide business decisions and strategies, often by collecting and analyzing large amounts of information.
nodes.why_it_matters: This is crucial because it enables organizations to make more informed decisions, optimize operations, and stay competitive in a data-rich environment.

nodes.label: Channel group analysis
nodes.source_sentence: Lately, if you look into the industry, um, these are the primary channel groups which they monitor.
nodes.description: Channel group analysis is the process of examining different sales or distribution channels to understand their performance and impact.
nodes.why_it_matters: Analyzing channel groups helps businesses identify which channels are most effective, allowing them to allocate resources and strategies more efficiently.

nodes.label: Bias in data-driven decision making
nodes.source_sentence: Again, one of the big problems with we go into analysing existing datasets as they will reflect existing behaviour patterns and existing behaviour patterns, especially in the real world, will build in all of the biases in those sorts of things which we're trying to get out of it.
nodes.description: Bias in data-driven decision making refers to the influence of existing patterns or prejudices in data, which can lead to unfair or inaccurate outcomes.
nodes.why_it_matters: Recognizing bias is important because it ensures that data-driven strategies lead to fair and accurate decisions, rather than reinforcing existing problems.
